section.title: What computation can know, prove, and conceal
section.deck: Avi Wigderson connects complexity, randomness, zero-knowledge proofs, quantum models, and the daily practice of theoretical research.

blocks.text: This conversation moves from the difference between finding and checking a solution to a deeper question: what resources make knowledge possible? Wigderson repeatedly changes the model or the resource being measured. The resulting distinctions matter: worst-case hardness differs from practical performance; computational unpredictability differs from true entropy; an interactive proof differs from an ordinary algorithm that decides a problem. The explanations below retain those boundaries and the assumptions behind the surprising results.

blocks.question: What is P versus NP, and why connect it to the limits of knowledge?
answer: P concerns problems that can be solved efficiently; NP concerns problems for which a proposed solution can be checked efficiently. Here, efficiency means polynomial growth in the input size. The question asks whether efficient checking always implies efficient solving.

Wigderson gives a philosophical interpretation: many serious searches aim at something we expect to recognize when we find it. A mathematician checks a proof, a scientist checks whether an explanation fits data, and an engineer checks whether a design meets its constraints. Finding an answer can be much harder than recognizing a satisfactory one.

He therefore presents P versus NP as a question about the reach of discovery. If the two classes were equal, efficiently verifiable solutions would also be efficiently findable in the formal setting. His references to human knowledge and a cure for cancer illustrate the significance he sees in the question; they should be read as a broad analogy, rather than a claim that every medical or human problem is literally an NP decision problem.
blocks.speaker: Avi Wigderson

blocks.question: Which answer do you expect, and why?
answer: He expects P and NP to differ, while stressing that the reasons are intuition, rather than a proof. Looking for lost keys feels harder than recognizing them once someone points them out. Many independently motivated optimization, logic, and verification problems have resisted attempts to find efficient general algorithms over decades.

NP-complete problems connect these searches: an efficient algorithm for one would give efficient algorithms for all problems in NP through reductions. Many appear to require searching an exponentially large space, and researchers do not see a general way to compress that search enough.

Those observations are suggestive, but a new idea could overturn them. His uncertainty is part of the answer: a long record of failure to find an algorithm is not a theorem that the algorithm cannot exist.
blocks.speaker: Avi Wigderson

blocks.question: Does NP-completeness mean practical software can do no better than brute force?
answer: The formal question requires an algorithm to be correct and efficient on every instance in a family. Real applications often produce a restricted set of instances with extra structure. A method can work very well on those instances while remaining poor in the worst case.

He uses protein folding as an illustration. A general energy-minimization formulation can be hard, while natural proteins need not represent arbitrary instances of that formulation. He suggests that evolution may have selected proteins with useful structure, and explicitly does not claim to know the biological explanation.

Similarly, verification formulas can contain structure that a SAT solver exploits. The simplex method offers another example: its worst-case running time can be exponential, despite strong practical performance. The existence of efficient general algorithms for linear programming is a separate point. Practical success and worst-case complexity answer different questions.
blocks.speaker: Avi Wigderson

blocks.question: Can relaxing exact correctness make a hard problem easy?
answer: It can help, but there is no universal guarantee. AlphaFold’s success on natural protein instances belongs to the structured-instance discussion; it does not settle the general worst-case optimization problem, even if its predictions work well on those inputs.

Approximation is another natural relaxation: accept a solution within a factor or percentage of the optimum. Wigderson explains that the PCP theorem and subsequent results also establish limits on approximation for many constraint problems.

For the MAX-3SAT example he describes, a random assignment satisfies a clause with probability 7/8. In the relevant worst-case approximation setting, guaranteeing even a small improvement beyond the 7/8 threshold is NP-hard. The striking point is that a modest-looking improvement over a simple baseline can already capture the difficult part of the problem.
blocks.speaker: Avi Wigderson

blocks.title: Three different kinds of success
rows: Does a heuristic work on useful inputs?
Good performance on the instances being tested or encountered.
An efficient correct method for every possible instance.
Can an approximation meet a guarantee?
A specified distance from the optimum in the stated setting.
A better guarantee beyond a hardness threshold.
Is there a polynomial-time general algorithm?
Efficient solution across the formal input family.
Whether it is the simplest or fastest choice on a particular application.

blocks.question: What is the wider landscape of complexity classes?
answer: Classes organize problems by resources and models. Time is one resource, but memory, communication between parties, energy, and parallel computation also matter. A problem can require different amounts of these resources, and adding more computers does not automatically make every computation immediate.
There is also a boundary before efficient computation: some problems are decidable at all, while others are not. P and NP describe a particular part of a much larger landscape.

Reductions relate problems even when their precise complexity is unknown. An efficient translation can turn a solver for one problem into a solver for another. His Sudoku example concerns the generalized family of growing puzzles, not a single fixed-size puzzle. Such relationships produce an ordering of difficulty and explain why very different-looking problems can belong together.
blocks.speaker: Avi Wigderson

blocks.question: How can very different problems reduce to satisfiability?
answer: Many basic reductions are relatively simple, although some major results, such as approximation hardness, require much deeper tools. The key intuition behind the foundational satisfiability reduction is that computation is local.

Imagine a proposed table of a machine’s states over time. Each step makes a small permitted change. Constraints can check the local transitions, the initial input, and the accepting outcome. A satisfying assignment then describes a consistent computation. What looked like an entire execution becomes a collection of small conditions that must all hold.

Other problems already have local constraints: graph coloring asks adjacent vertices to receive different colors. Factoring also illustrates verification: multiply proposed factors and check the product. Encoding that multiplication gives a satisfiability instance. Reducibility to SAT does not by itself say that factoring is NP-complete.
blocks.speaker: Avi Wigderson

blocks.title: Turning a proposed computation into constraints

steps.title: Describe the input
steps.text: Fix the initial information the computation must use.

steps.title: Propose the execution
steps.text: Represent a sequence of machine states.

steps.title: Check local steps
steps.text: Require each small transition to obey the computation rules.

steps.title: Check the outcome
steps.text: Require the resulting sequence to satisfy the target condition.

blocks.caption: An editorial outline of the locality intuition behind the satisfiability reduction.

blocks.question: Is there a general theory of trading time against space?
answer: Yes, but the answer depends on the problem and the model of computation. Some results force a tradeoff between small memory and fast execution; other problems permit both. Models that are equivalent in what they can compute need not be equivalent when exact resource costs matter.

A basic observation is that a computation running for t steps cannot visit more than t memory locations. He then describes space-saving simulation results: earlier work improved the direct bound, and a result by Ryan Williams achieved a much larger, roughly square-root-scale saving in the Turing-machine setting. The time cost of these simulations can become very large. This is a statement about what a model permits, rather than a ready-made optimization for arbitrary programs.

followups.question: Does that result apply to a general computation?
answer: He specifies Turing machines and cautions that the same statement may not apply to random-access machines. The model is part of the theorem.

followups.question: Is there an intuitive example of how such unexpected space savings work?
answer: Instead of unpacking the newer proof, he gives an older example associated with Barrington: a majority decision can be represented using a very small internal state and an appropriate sequence of repeated accesses to input bits. The surprising question is whether there are more zeros or ones, rather than the task of printing their exact count.

The explanation uses noncommuting permutations: rotating and then flipping can differ from flipping and then rotating. Carefully arranged operations can simulate logical gates. He offers a picture-hanging puzzle as an analogy: loop a string around two nails so removing either nail drops the picture. The interview poses that puzzle but does not work through its solution.

This is an explanation of a particular branching-program viewpoint. The small internal state does not mean that every ordinary computer can inspect an arbitrary input with no addressing or control resources.

followups.question: Is the information encoded in the sequence of operations?
answer: That is the intuition, with an important output distinction. A yes-or-no majority answer is small; printing an arbitrarily large count would itself require enough bits to represent that count. He adds that this line of work has useful applications, including in cryptography, rather than being only an abstract curiosity.

blocks.speaker: Avi Wigderson

blocks.question: Why use a SAT solver if translating the problem can enlarge it?
answer: A translation may indeed make the instance larger. But satisfiability has received an enormous amount of practical optimization. Heuristics select influential variables whose assignments force other choices, sometimes producing a cascade that sharply reduces the search space.

Those methods exploit structure rather than escaping all worst-case hardness. He also mentions the stronger conjectural expectation that difficult satisfiability instances require exponential time. That is an expectation about hard cases, not a description of every formula.

For verification, the translation is often convenient because specifications already look like sets of constraints. The cost of moving into SAT can be outweighed by the maturity of the solver and the fit between the specification and its input language.
blocks.speaker: Avi Wigderson

blocks.question: Why treat randomness as a computational resource?
answer: Random choices can make algorithms effective; randomized primality testing is one historical example. Their analysis commonly assumes perfectly unbiased, independent bits. Actual computers need a source for those bits, and obtaining high-quality randomness has a cost.

Physical noise, traffic measurements, deterministic generators, and digits of a mathematical constant are different proposals, not interchangeable proofs of ideal randomness. Quantum measurements offer another source in the physical model, but a real device still costs money and has imperfections.

Once randomness is a resource, researchers can ask how many bits an algorithm needs, what quality it uses, and whether its error can be reduced or its random choices removed. Sometimes the analysis requires far less independence than it first appears to require. He describes the discovery of deterministic primality testing as an example of understanding the way randomness was being used, rather than simply supplying more of it.
blocks.speaker: Avi Wigderson

blocks.question: How do you quantify the quality of random bits?
answer: For pseudorandomness, quality is relative to a test or observer. The goal is for the relevant algorithm not to distinguish a lower-entropy generated distribution from the ideal random one. Different algorithms can require different kinds of pseudorandomness.

For some analyses, pairwise or limited higher-order independence is enough. A much smaller seed can then generate the distribution the algorithm needs. The practical question is what the analysis actually demands, rather than whether the output is random by every possible definition.

followups.question: What makes randomness depend on the observer’s computational power?
answer: Consider predicting the landing of the same tossed coin. An unaided observer has little basis for doing better than a guess. A laptop alone may not help in the tiny time window. Sensors and sufficient computation, in the thought experiment, could measure the conditions and predict the motion.
The event has not changed; the observer’s ability has. This illustrates computational uncertainty. It does not say that physical entropy itself changes because a faster computer is present.

blocks.speaker: Avi Wigderson

blocks.question: Under what assumptions can randomness be removed from efficient algorithms?
answer: He describes the hardness-versus-randomness connection: sufficiently strong computational hardness assumptions can yield pseudorandom generators and imply P = BPP, meaning efficient bounded-error randomized computation can be simulated efficiently without randomness.

The assumption he describes concerns strong circuit hardness, such as exponential circuit requirements. It is stronger and more specific than merely stating P ≠ NP. The surprising relationship is that an assumption about difficulty, with no randomness in its wording, can support the removal of randomness.

He also explains that the connection has converse forms: successful derandomization can imply hardness results. The exact relationship depends on the version of the theorem; he does not present one unconditional equivalence covering every setting.
blocks.speaker: Avi Wigderson

blocks.question: What is the intuition connecting hardness and randomness?
answer: A computationally limited observer cannot always determine the answer to a hard problem, so there is uncertainty relative to that observer. But having a few hard instances is not enough: the construction needs answers that are difficult to predict on average, almost like fair coin flips. Hardness amplification strengthens that unpredictability.
Producing one unpredictable answer from many random input bits still does not expand randomness. A generator must do the reverse: use a short seed to produce many outputs that look random together.

He describes the Nisan–Wigderson approach at a high level: evaluate a hard function on carefully chosen subsets of a short seed. The output bits may be mathematically correlated, yet the restricted observer cannot detect the correlation. The guarantee remains conditional on the relevant hardness and the observer’s computational limit.
blocks.speaker: Avi Wigderson

blocks.question: With unlimited computation, would nothing be truly random?
answer: An unrestricted observer could distinguish an expanded low-entropy seed distribution from a fully uniform one. That shows the limit of a computational pseudorandomness guarantee.

It does not eliminate information-theoretic randomness. A task that demands a genuinely random bit or a specified amount of entropy is asking something different from fooling a limited test. He uses secrets and security as motivation for caring about entropy itself. The correct notion depends on the task; the coin-prediction analogy does not establish that unlimited computation can predict every physical phenomenon.
blocks.speaker: Avi Wigderson

blocks.question: How can weak sources produce better randomness?
answer: Randomness extraction is a different, though related, theory. A weak source can contain uncertainty while also having bias and correlations. Weather is an intuitive example: tomorrow is not fully predictable, but it is correlated with today. Feeding arbitrary weak bits directly to an algorithm that expects independent fair bits can make it fail.

The difficult part is that the entropy may be present without its location or structure being known. A universal deterministic procedure cannot simply turn every arbitrary single weak source into one perfect output string.

He describes a way around that obstacle for running algorithms: generate a collection of candidate blocks, with most having the useful randomness guarantee in the relevant construction, run the algorithm on the candidates, and combine the answers by a majority vote. The details depend on the extraction model and assumptions. This is an intuition for computational use, rather than an instruction for manufacturing a secret by choosing any one candidate.

followups.question: What is the idea behind constructions with several sources and sum–product structure?
answer: With several independent weak sources, the goal can be to combine them into a source with more useful entropy. He relates this to arithmetic combinatorics. Adding every pair in an arithmetic progression may produce little growth; multiplying every pair in a geometric progression may also produce little growth. Sum–product results capture the fact that the two operations cannot both remain similarly unproductive in the relevant setting.

Mixing multiplication and addition, such as multiplying two source values and adding a third, can exploit that tension. A full proof must analyze distributions and entropy, not just count distinct values. He explicitly separates this multi-source intuition from the harder arbitrary single-source problem.

blocks.speaker: Avi Wigderson

blocks.question: What is a zero-knowledge proof?
answer: First enlarge the idea of a proof. Instead of sending one written object for a verifier to check, a prover and a randomized verifier can interact. A sound protocol makes the chance of accepting a false claim very small.

Zero knowledge adds a privacy requirement: the verifier becomes convinced of the claim without learning the secret proof or witness beyond what the claim itself reveals. A cryptographic participant might need to show that a public number was produced by multiplying two primes, while keeping those primes secret. More generally, participants want assurance that others followed a protocol without exposing their private inputs.

Wigderson recalls how implausible this initially sounded. His work showed the broad reach of the idea for efficiently verifiable claims under the required cryptographic assumptions. The surprise is that convincing someone and revealing the underlying secret need not be the same act.
blocks.speaker: Avi Wigderson

blocks.question: How can a proof be checked without revealing it?
answer: The explanation assumes suitable one-way functions: easy to compute in one direction and hard to invert. These support commitments with two important properties. Hiding prevents the other person from learning the committed value; binding prevents the sender from later changing the value they claim to have committed to.

For the example, both people know a graph and the prover knows a legal three-coloring. The prover commits to a color at every vertex. The verifier randomly chooses an edge, and the prover opens the commitments at its endpoints. The verifier checks that both colors are allowed and are different.

If the graph cannot be legally colored, every proposed coloring has a defect. Random checks have a chance of exposing it, and repetition makes the chance of undetected cheating very small. But reusing the same coloring would gradually disclose it. The prover therefore randomly renames the three colors before each round. The two opened colors then look like a random pair of different colors, rather than pieces of one stable secret assignment.

Finally, reductions make the example broadly useful. A reduction must translate the original instance and its witness into a graph and a corresponding legal coloring. An efficiently checkable proof can be handled through that representation. The interview gives the intuition; the formal zero-knowledge definition and security proof require more care than this sketch.

followups.question: Can the verifier ever be completely certain?
answer: The completeness side can be exact: an honest prover with the required witness succeeds. Soundness against a dishonest prover can retain a nonzero error probability, reduced to an arbitrarily small level by repetition. Those are different guarantees.

blocks.speaker: Avi Wigderson

blocks.title: The graph-coloring proof sketch

steps.title: Hide a valid assignment
steps.text: Commit to all vertex colors after randomly renaming them.

steps.title: Choose a surprise check
steps.text: Let the verifier select an edge at random.

steps.title: Reveal a tiny part
steps.text: Open only that edge’s endpoint commitments and check different valid colors.

steps.title: Repeat with new hiding
steps.text: Use fresh commitments and a new color permutation to reduce cheating risk without accumulating the assignment.

blocks.caption: An editorial illustration of the conditional, high-level protocol explained in the interview.

blocks.question: How has quantum computation changed complexity theory?
answer: Quantum computation adds operations inspired by quantum mechanics, including superposition and interference. Interference permits contributions to reinforce or cancel; the interview’s analogy with negative numbers is about that behavior, rather than negative probabilities. Measuring suitable quantum states also supplies random bits, so the model includes randomized computation.

Shor’s efficient algorithms for factoring and discrete logarithms made the significance concrete. They threatened specific assumptions used in important public-key systems and stimulated both hardware work and cryptographic research. Building the machinery is a separate challenge: maintaining quantum states, controlling noise and decoherence, and correcting errors are difficult engineering problems.

Cryptography must ask which assumptions survive a quantum adversary. He distinguishes plentiful intuitions about one-way processes from the rarer structures needed for useful trapdoor systems. He discusses lattice-based problems and learning with errors as candidates for which efficient quantum algorithms were not known in the conversation’s context. Lack of a known attack remains an assumption, rather than a proof of security.

The effects extend beyond cryptography. Quantum models bring computer scientists and physicists together, suggest algorithms that can sometimes be translated back into classical approaches, and create new questions about proof systems.

His most striking example is MIP* = RE, involving multiple entangled provers and an efficient verifier in a particular interactive proof model. That model can verify claims connected with undecidable problems. It does not give an ordinary algorithm that decides the halting problem. He emphasizes that the techniques also resolve important mathematical questions: a model that initially seems remote can produce useful new proof methods.

followups.question: How can a verifier handle something described as undecidable?
answer: He does not offer a short derivation. The result depends on a very substantial body of work combining quantum proof systems with classical techniques, coding theory, algebra, and PCP ideas. The long proof adds more tools on top of that foundation. The remarkable claim belongs to the specific interactive model, whose assumptions must remain visible.

blocks.speaker: Avi Wigderson

blocks.question: How does the community verify an extremely long, surprising proof?
answer: Carefully, and sometimes over years. Wigderson compares the process with other major mathematical proofs that required extended checking, corrections, and explanatory work. For the quantum proof-system result, he describes an early bug that was fixed, ongoing refereeing at the time of the conversation, and later papers that reused the tools or supplied alternative and stronger results.

Confidence comes from people examining and extending the argument, rather than from the size or prestige of the initial paper. He also points toward formal proof systems such as Lean as a possible way to make parts of verification more explicit and machine-checkable. His remarks about the paper’s review status are historical to the interview.
blocks.speaker: Avi Wigderson

blocks.question: What is the relationship between mathematics and theoretical computer science?
answer: He sees the field as having two parents. Mathematics contributes rigorous theorems, proofs, and aesthetic questions. Computer science contributes the central object of computation and questions motivated by technology, industry, and natural systems.

The field asks what can arise from sequences of simple local steps and what resources those steps require. Similar questions can be posed about software, biological processes, and physical systems. Living between the two disciplines gives researchers both a supply of useful models and the freedom to study models for their own structure.
blocks.speaker: Avi Wigderson

blocks.question: What motivates you when an application is not the immediate goal?
answer: He first corrects the emphasis on solving problems: creating models, definitions, and questions is itself a central contribution. The computational definition of pseudorandomness is one example of a definition opening an unexpected line of work.

His interest in computation is intrinsic and grew through a computer science education. He regrets not having studied more mathematics earlier, because he had to learn it later. He also values a lively, collaborative community in which colleagues have become close friends.

Applications can be surprising. He originally expected the general zero-knowledge protocol to be too expensive for implementation; motivated researchers found more practical approaches and different assumptions. The broader lesson is to investigate a natural theoretical question without demanding that its first formulation be immediately deployable.

Some foundational questions still have no direct system implementation. Establishing strong hardness results could move cryptography from assumptions toward theorems, but the limits of efficient computation remain poorly understood. He regards the field as being early in its understanding, despite the substantial structure it has already built.
blocks.speaker: Avi Wigderson

blocks.question: What is it like to make rare major discoveries?
answer: The experience is exceptional, but most progress consists of small contributions from a community of researchers. Papers strengthen bounds, adapt techniques, or clarify one piece of an argument. He considers that incremental work essential.

A breakthrough need not settle a famous decades-old question. It can expose an unexpected possibility, as in the small-state majority example: he recalls that the researcher had been trying to prove an impossibility when the new approach appeared.

The day-to-day practice matters more than a distant prize. Many days end without solving the intended problem. Failed attempts can still teach something that later becomes useful. The work suits people who enjoy thinking, trying ideas, and learning through that uncertainty; it will not satisfy everyone in the same way.
blocks.speaker: Avi Wigderson

blocks.question: What advice would you give a beginning researcher?
answer: He would not change much about his own path, which he attributes partly to luck: excellent mentors, collaborators, and a community welcoming to young researchers. As a first-year graduate student, he remembers a senior figure taking genuine interest in the problem he had studied.

His actionable advice is to explore a variety of areas and work on the problems you enjoy most. A prestigious target may not match your affinity. Reading across areas and trying several kinds of problems helps reveal both interests and capabilities; the work you enjoy can also be the work you do best.
blocks.speaker: Avi Wigderson
